What are noble metals?

Noble metals are metals that show relatively low chemical reactivity and resist oxidation or corrosion under many ordinary conditions. Gold, silver and platinum are familiar examples.

Gold is particularly resistant to reaction with oxygen and moisture, which helps it retain its appearance. Platinum is also highly resistant to many chemical reactions. Silver is comparatively unreactive but can develop a black coating of silver sulphide when exposed to sulphur-containing substances in air.

Thus, noble does not mean completely unreactive. It indicates relative chemical resistance, not an inability to react under all conditions.

Gold and aqua regia

Gold does not ordinarily react with dilute hydrochloric acid or dilute sulphuric acid. It can, however, be dissolved by aqua regia, a mixture of concentrated hydrochloric acid and concentrated nitric acid in a 3:1 ratio by volume. This is an example of how a metal that resists many individual reagents can still react under special chemical conditions.

The important examination distinction is the unusual chemical resistance of gold, not the practical handling of corrosive reagents.

Why gold is used for jewellery

Gold has metallic lustre, high malleability, exceptional ductility and relatively low chemical reactivity. It can be shaped into intricate ornaments and retains its characteristic appearance for long periods.

However, very pure gold is soft and may not withstand everyday wear as well as a harder alloy. Therefore, copper, silver or other suitable metals are commonly added to gold used for jewellery.

Understanding gold karat and fineness

Karat, written K, expresses the proportion of gold in a gold alloy on a scale of 24 parts. On this scale, 24K represents pure gold in the idealised school-level explanation.

The theoretical relationship is:

Gold percentage = (Gold karat / 24) × 100

For example, 22K gold contains 22 parts gold out of 24 parts of alloy by mass:

22/24 × 100 = 91.67% approximately

The remaining approximately 8.33% consists of other alloying metals.

Fineness expresses the precious-metal content in parts per thousand. Thus, a fineness mark of 916 means at least 916 parts of gold per 1000 parts of alloy, corresponding to 91.6% gold.

Gold gradeNominal karat proportionCommon BIS fineness designation
24K24/24, ideally pure24KS995 or 24KF999, depending on specified grade
22K22/24, about 91.67%22K916
18K18/24, 75%18K750
14K14/24, about 58.33%14K585

The karat fractions provide the familiar school-level interpretation. The BIS fineness designations specify minimum gold content in parts per thousand. This is why the nominal calculation for 22K gives about 91.67%, whereas the mark 916 specifies 91.6% fineness. Similarly, 14K585 denotes a standard with at least 58.5% gold rather than an exact mathematical restatement of 14/24.

For 24K, the practical distinction is also important: 24KF999 denotes fine gold of at least 999 parts per thousand, while 24KS995 denotes standard gold of at least 995 parts per thousand. The label 24K alone should not be interpreted as a guarantee of absolutely 100% pure gold.

Gold purity is not the same as jewellery weight

If an ornament weighs 10 g and has 22K916 fineness, the minimum gold content indicated by that fineness is:

10 × 916/1000 = 9.16 g

The remaining mass is alloying material, assuming the stated 10 g is the net mass of the gold alloy and excludes stones or other non-gold components.

Thus, 10 g of a 22K916 alloy is not the same as 10 g of pure gold. The fineness tells us the proportion of gold, while the net weight tells us how much material is present.

Karat and carat are not interchangeable concepts: gold karat refers to purity, whereas carat in gemstone measurement refers to mass.

BIS hallmarking in India

The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) operates India's hallmarking system for precious-metal articles. Hallmarking provides an official indication that an article has been assessed for the stated purity or fineness.

According to BIS consumer guidance consulted on 3 November 2026, the hallmarking system for gold jewellery using the Hallmark Unique Identification system consists of 3 principal marks:

  1. BIS logo: Identifies the hallmarking system.
  2. Purity mark: Shows the gold grade in karat and fineness, such as 22K916 or 18K750.
  3. HUID: A unique 6-character alphanumeric identification code associated with the hallmarked item.

The 3-mark HUID system was introduced on 1 July 2021, replacing the earlier 4-mark format for newly hallmarked gold jewellery. The HUID can be checked through the Verify HUID feature in the BIS Care application.

BIS consumer guidance updated on 26 November 2025 describes the use of that verification facility. These are the stated features of the system at the selected content cutoff of 3 November 2026; they should not be confused with a claim that every gold article or every older ornament necessarily carries a HUID.

Hallmarking is a statement about purity, not about the total weight, jewellery design, making charges or the price of the ornament. A buyer must distinguish the purity mark from the weight recorded on the bill.

22K916 identifies gold of at least 916 parts per thousand. HUID identifies a hallmarked article. The 2 markings serve different purposes.

Connections across the chapter

The behaviour of metals and non-metals follows several connected principles:

  • Physical properties: Metals generally show lustre, malleability, ductility and conductivity, but exceptions include mercury, iodine and graphite.
  • Chemical properties: Metal oxides are generally basic, non-metal oxides often acidic, and some metal oxides amphoteric.
  • Reactivity: A more reactive metal generally displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution.
  • Bonding: Metals can lose electrons and non-metals gain them to form ionic compounds, which conduct when ions can move.
  • Extraction: Highly reactive metals commonly require electrolysis; moderately reactive metals are often obtained by reduction of their oxides.
  • Corrosion and alloys: Protective coatings and suitable alloying improve the usefulness and durability of metals.
  • Gold purity: Gold's low reactivity makes it valuable, while alloying improves hardness and fineness indicates its gold content.

Prelims focus

  • Gold, silver and platinum are familiar noble metals.
  • Silver may tarnish even though it is relatively unreactive.
  • 24K denotes very pure gold; 22K is commonly alloyed for jewellery.
  • 22K916 means at least 91.6% gold; 18K750 means at least 75% gold.
  • A BIS HUID is a 6-character alphanumeric identifier.
  • Trap: Gold purity, net jewellery weight and HUID are 3 different concepts.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 3, Metals and Non-metals, Sections 3.1, 3.2.3, 3.4 and 3.5.1, pp. 38–54; Bureau of Indian Standards, IS 1417:2016, Gold and Gold Alloys, Jewellery/Artefacts—Fineness and Marking, official Summary of Indian Standards, section on grades of fineness; Bureau of Indian Standards, General Hallmarking FAQs, questions 1, 4, 8 and 9, accessed 3 November 2026; Bureau of Indian Standards, Consumer Protection, section Verification of HUID by BIS Care App, updated 26 November 2025, accessed 3 November 2026.]
